title: Navigating uncertain waters: a critical review of inferring foraging behaviour from location and dive data in pinnipeds

subsections.subsection_title: Physiological Foundations of Diving and Foraging Capacity
subsections.content:
The need to find food is a fundamental pressure that drives the evolution of animal physiology, behaviour, and life histories ref [1]. A key question for ecologists is how animals exploit their environment to optimise prey intake and maximise fitness ref [1]. For air-breathing diving predators, such as marine mammals, sea turtles, and seabirds, foraging poses a unique challenge: within the physiological constraints of breath-hold, individuals must find patchily-distributed prey resources in a three dimensional (3D) dynamic environment ref [2]. Observing and measuring such behaviour in the field is inherently problematic. However, in recent years, a suite of devices and analytical techniques dedicated to tackling this challenge has emerged ref [3]ref [4]ref [10]ref [13].

Although technological advances are allowing us to minimise the size and weight of biologging devices, there is substantial evidence to suggest that some methods of handling animals for tag application, and the physical effects of the tag itself, may alter the subsequent behaviour of the individual, and perhaps its prey ref [131]ref [132]ref [133]ref [134]. For example, head-mounted cameras with strobe flashes have been reported to affect the diving behaviour of their pinniped carriers, and/or the prey on which they forage ref [131]. In contrast to flying seabirds, where device weight can have a large effect on the energetics of flight ref [135], drag caused by tag placement is a greater concern in pinnipeds ref [136]. Hazekamp et al. ref [132] showed that externally-attached devices such as SRDLs can change an animal's hydrodynamics and potentially alter their physiology and behaviour. Tag designers face a challenge in that a device's antenna must break the surface in order to receive a location estimate and/or transmit data. This often requires tag placement on the head, neck or back. Attaching tags in a caudal position would likely reduce device-induced turbulence ref [137], however this would compromise data collection and transmission. Whilst the effects on animals will only last as long as the device is attached, ecologists should be mindful that the movement patterns observed in their data may carry some bias. In addition to these concerns, this also raises ethical considerations about the welfare of the individual, particularly for juveniles and smaller species, in which drag effects may be more severe ref [138]. As we continue to rely on biologging data to inform the conservation management of species, more research is urgently needed in this field in order to assess the potential bias in existing datasets, refine capture and tag application methods, and improve the hydrodynamic footprint of externally-attached devices.

subsections.subsection_title: Instrumentation Effects and Ethical Considerations in Tagging
subsections.content: For many years knowledge of pinniped movements was limited to re-sightings of coded mark-recapture flipper tags or brandings ref [27] (Fig. 1a-b). These observations allow long-term monitoring of survival and dispersal, but offer little insight into where individuals go between hauling-out. Many technological options are now available for tracking animal movement at sea (Table 1; Fig. 1). In this review we focus on devices capable of collecting fine-scale information on foraging movements. Whilst global location sensors (GLS) and smart position or temperature transmitters (SPOT) have been used in foraging studies, they are generally deployed to track migration or broadscale movement, and foraging inferences are made from behavioural data or higher resolution location data from simultaneously-deployed devices ref [28]ref [29]ref [30]. GLS and SPOT tags are therefore excluded from this review.

subsections.subsection_title: Biologging Technologies for Monitoring Pinniped Behavior
subsections.content:
Foraging can be classified at the scale of surface movement patterns, individual dives, or even parts of dives. With all attempts to infer foraging from tracking data there are important considerations to be made. Firstly, models should ideally detect foraging on the scale of search of the individual. For animals with small ranges of movement, detecting search behaviour may require data at high levels of spatial and temporal resolution. The scale of movement may therefore be too fine to detect with data transmitted via Argos, and researchers may find that model parameters are defined by the data resolution rather than the biology ref [10, 64, 83, 110]. This may result in under/over-estimation of foraging. For example, a recent study used SSMs to compare activity budgets for grey and harbour seals ref [121]. The study combined Argos SRDL data with GPS-GSM data. In order to utilise both data types, SSMs were fit to assign movement states to 6 h intervals. Whilst the resolution was suitable to quantify activity budgets for grey seals, determining between travel and foraging proved problematic for harbour seals, probably because they typically forage closer to shore, and thus do not exhibit long periods of travelling ref [121]. The SSM models for harbour seals performed better when GPS data were used on a 2 h resolution interval ref [129]. Secondly, the research question will also dictate the resolution of data required; in order to investigate the fine-scale movements of harbour seals within an offshore windfarm, Russell et. al. ref [130] used an SSM with fifteen minute intervals. In this case, with a 2 h interval, it would not be possible to determine if individuals trace specific structures, or to distinguish between foraging and travelling around and between these structures. For long-ranging species moving across ocean basins, in which behaviour may switch between migration and residency, a small number of location fixes per day may be enough to detect discrete behaviours. Therefore, when designing tagging studies, researchers should be mindful of the spatial and temporal data resolution required to accurately identify changes in movement patterns for their study species and research question, and choose a device and sampling rate that will capture this signal ( Fig. 6; ref [64]). Nevertheless, increasing duty cycles will likely have a negative effect on the duration of the battery, and so, the trade-off between sampling frequency and duration needs to be carefully considered ref [7].

The deployment of animal-borne telemetry and data logging devices has enabled unprecedented quantification of movement, behaviour, and physiology in pinnipeds at finer spatial and temporal scales than ever before ref [2, 3]. Technologies such as CTD-Satellite Relay Data Loggers (CTD-SRDLs) now allow real-time collection of oceanographic data alongside behavioural metrics, enhancing the ecological context of foraging inferences ref [6]. These instruments, often deployed on long-ranging species like northern elephant seals, provide high-resolution depth, temperature, and salinity profiles that complement movement data and support multi-dimensional foraging analyses ref [5]. The increasing use of accelerometry and state-space modelling in biologging studies reflects broader methodological advances in detecting behavioural states from complex datasets ref [2, 3]. Moreover, the design and programming of electronic tracking tags critically influence data quality, particularly for small-scale movements where frequent, regular sampling is essential to recover true behavioural patterns ref [10]. The widespread adoption of biologging in diving studies underscores its centrality to understanding pinniped foraging ecology, though limitations in tag size, energy constraints, and data transmission fidelity remain persistent challenges ref [4, 7].

subsections.subsection_title: Challenges in Spatial Accuracy and Data Interpretation
subsections.content: The spatial accuracy of location data acquired via satellite telemetry systems, particularly ARGOS, remains a critical constraint in interpreting pinniped foraging behavior, as location errors can distort movement paths and misrepresent habitat use patterns ref [19]. These errors are exacerbated by the high proportion of low-accuracy location classes (LC 0, A, B) generated during underwater dives, which are common in pinniped diving ecology ref [23]. While filtering techniques and state-space models have been developed to correct for these errors, their efficacy varies significantly depending on the underlying error structure and the species' movement dynamics ref [20]. The Argos-CLS Kalman Filter, introduced to improve location accuracy over traditional least squares methods, has demonstrated measurable reductions in positional error when validated against Fastloc GPS data, though residual biases persist ref [21]. Bayesian state-space models fitted to Kalman-filtered ARGOS data have shown up to a 27% improvement in location accuracy compared to models fitted to least squares data, with 82% of predicted locations falling within 5 km of true GPS positions ref [22]. However, even with advanced correction methods, the temporal sampling rate dictated by satellite pass frequency and the spatial error inherent in ARGOS transmissions can severely limit the detection of area-restricted search behavior, particularly at fine spatial scales (<10 km) ref [8]. Furthermore, the ratio of longitude to latitude error in ARGOS locations is often asymmetric, with longitude errors consistently higher across most location classes, which can bias directional interpretations of foraging paths ref [23]. The choice of attachment method, data transmission frequency, and tag retrieval strategy further modulates the quality and completeness of spatial datasets, influencing the reliability of behavioral inferences ref [19]. Consequently, without rigorous validation against high-accuracy GPS data, spatial interpretations of pinniped foraging behavior derived from ARGOS telemetry remain inherently uncertain ref [20].

subsections.subsection_title: Validating Foraging Inferences from Dive and Movement Data
subsections.content:
Choosing the appropriate analytical method will depend upon careful consideration of some key aspects of the study. Key aspects are given in bold, subsequent considerations are shown in parentheses (duty cycle, battery duration, quantity of data, data acquisition / transmission opportunities) Fig. 6

Validating foraging inferences from dive and movement data requires direct observation or proxy measures of prey capture, as dive patterns alone may not reliably indicate feeding events. Studies using animal-borne video have demonstrated that descent rate is a strong predictor of prey capture attempts in Australian fur seals, with models achieving up to 77.5% accuracy in classifying dives as containing prey capture events ref [29]. Similarly, head-mounted accelerometers have been validated against video to identify prey capture signatures in the same species, confirming that accelerometry can detect fine-scale feeding behaviors with high fidelity ref [25]. In penguins, supervised machine learning applied to accelerometry data successfully classified prey handling events with 84.95% accuracy, providing a robust framework for inferring foraging success in wild populations ref [26]. For northern elephant seals, stomach temperature recorders have been used to validate that reduced transit rates correlate significantly with feeding events, establishing a behavioral proxy for foraging ref [27]. Further, jaw-motion recorders in elephant seals have revealed high frequencies of feeding attempts linked to mesopelagic prey, demonstrating that dive duration and depth alone are insufficient without direct measures of jaw activity ref [30]. In Antarctic fur seals, prey capture attempts detected via Hall sensors showed that descent and ascent rates at the dive scale, and bottom duration at coarser temporal scales, best predict foraging intensity, highlighting the importance of scale-dependent modeling ref [28]. These studies collectively underscore that while dive characteristics such as bottom duration, descent rate, and ascent rate are commonly used proxies, their predictive power varies across species, scales, and ecological contexts, and must be validated against direct or indirect measures of prey capture ref [25], ref [26], ref [27], ref [28], ref [29], ref [30].

subsections.section_title: Inferring Foraging Behaviour from Single Data Types
subsections.subsection_title: Inferring Foraging from Dive Profiles: Validations and Limitations
subsections.content: Methods of inferring foraging from the data described above generally fall into three categories: (i) use of dive data, (ii) use of location data, and (iii) consideration of movements in three dimensions. Dive profiles, particularly bottom duration and descent/ascent rates, have been widely used as proxies for foraging success, with validation studies demonstrating their predictive power across multiple pinniped species ref [28], ref [29]. For instance, in Antarctic fur seals, descent and ascent rates at the dive scale, and bottom duration at longer temporal scales, were strong predictors of prey capture attempts ref [28], while in Australian fur seals, descent rate alone was sufficient to predict dives containing prey capture attempts with 77.5% accuracy ref [29]. The assumption that foraging occurs predominantly during the bottom phase has been challenged by high-resolution data revealing complex within-dive behavioral segmentation, where hunting phases—identified by vertical sinuosity—account for up to 77% of prey capture attempts, even when occurring outside the traditional bottom phase ref [27]. Dive shape classification, such as U-shaped, V-shaped, and square-wave profiles, has also been linked to foraging behavior, with U-shaped dives associated with foraging in harbour seals ref [31] and square-wave dives linked to benthic foraging in grey seals ref [10]. Comparative analyses across 12 pinniped and seabird species confirm that square dives are the most common profile, suggesting a conserved foraging strategy across taxa ref [11]. Furthermore, three-dimensional movement analyses in ringed seals reveal that local search behavior, inferred from grid cell revisits and reduced swimming speed, occurs disproportionately during the bottom phase (41% of bottom phases vs. <10% of descents/ascents), reinforcing the utility of dive phase analysis for identifying foraging ref [16]. However, the relationship between dive metrics and foraging is not universal; temporal scale, species-specific foraging ecology, and behavioral context (e.g., breeding vs. migration) significantly modulate these associations ref [28], ref [29], ref [33]. For example, in northern elephant seals, feeding events occurred across all dive types but were most frequent during foraging-type dive shapes, and were negatively correlated with transit rate, indicating that behavioral state transitions must be considered alongside dive metrics ref [33]. Thus, while dive profiles offer a powerful and widely applicable tool for inferring foraging, their interpretation requires careful validation against direct behavioral data and consideration of ecological and temporal context.

subsections.section_title: Inferring Foraging Behaviour from Single Data Types
subsections.subsection_title: Direct Validation of Foraging Events Using Accelerometry and Video
subsections.content:
In VHF studies during the early 1990s, the presence of diving was used to infer foraging activity in pinnipeds ref [32]. However, seals may dive for reasons other than searching for prey. For example, individuals may dive for efficient travel ref [31], and some species also perform resting or digestion dives ref [31, 35, 65, 66]. Diving datasets collected using pressure sensors can be applied in various ways to infer foraging. From each dive, a number of empirical and geometric measurements can be calculated, including the duration of the dive; duration of bottom time; maximum depth; duration of surface interval; ascent and descent rates; distribution of time allocation across depths (Time Allocation at Depth (TAD) index; see Glossary (Additional file 1)); and 2D dive profile shapes (Fig. 3). The application of each of these metrics depends on the resolution of the data, the temporal scale of analysis, and the specific research question (i.e. whether the study aims to quantify search activity, successful foraging or other aspects of behaviour and physiology). Direct validation of foraging events using accelerometry and video has demonstrated that head-mounted accelerometers can detect prey capture events with high accuracy, revealing distinct jerk signatures associated with raptorial and suction feeding ref [2], and enabling the identification of prey captures in Australian fur seals through synchronized video validation ref [1].

These approaches have moved beyond inferring foraging from dive shape alone, providing direct evidence of feeding behavior and clarifying the limitations of proxy-based inferences.

subsections.section_title: Inferring Foraging Behaviour from Single Data Types
subsections.subsection_title: Dive Behavior as a Proxy for Foraging Effort and Success
subsections.content:
Animal location data can be used to identify and quantify foraging. For central place foragers that make discrete foraging trips to sea, returning to land to rest and digest, or provision young, the duration and extent of these trips are used to make broad observations of foraging effort ref [102]ref [103]ref [104]. However, in isolation, trip duration and extent give no information about where individuals are searching for prey, how they are exploiting their environment in order to find it, what proportion of the time at sea is spent foraging in relation to other behaviours such as resting and travelling, and if they are foraging successfully. Within the trip itself, the distribution of time along the track can be analysed, and movement patterns that may relate to specific behaviours can be identified ref [105]. The simplest way to deconstruct a horizontal track and identify movement patterns is to divide it into segments of straight lines interrupted by turns. In order to quantify the distribution of time along a track, it is often necessary to regularise 'fixes' (locations) to a constant time step (Fig. 4a). By interpolating between temporally-regularised locations, the displacement distance and change in bearing between fixes can then be extracted (Fig. 4b). Displacement gives a measure of ground speed, whilst change in bearing (turning angle) can show track sinuosity. Predator movements are often classified into two broad strategies; ref [1] 'directed' travel with little or no meandering, and ref [2] 'resident' behaviour with slower, meandering movement (Fig. 5a) ref [105, 106]. In the context of OFT, these slower movements are commonly attributed to area-restricted search (ARS) behaviour, indicative of foraging effort within a prey patch ref [105, 107, 108]. Studies commonly use track metrics to distinguish between directed and resident movement patterns. For example, travel to and from, or between, foraging patches is associated with high displacement between fixes, and small changes in bearing. In contrast, ARS behaviour is characterised by a more sinuous track section with lower displacement ref [105]. Although opportunistic foraging may occur during directed travel ref [15, 31, 109], and individuals may search for prey on multiple spatial scales ref [108, 110], ARS behaviour is often used to quantify when and where predators concentrate foraging effort. Methods of quantifying ARS from track metrics range from simple descriptive approaches (e.g. plotting variable distributions through time and defining a threshold ref [106]) to sophisticated mechanistic models that can incorporate multiple movement metrics at different data resolutions and account for spatial uncertainty of location estimates ref [111].

The physiological and biomechanical constraints on foraging efficiency are further modulated by body condition and metabolic limits. For instance, blubber thickness influences buoyancy during dives, which in turn affects the energy cost of locomotion and the interpretation of dive profiles as proxies for foraging effort; fatter seals exhibit higher drift rates during passive descent, which can be used to monitor changes in body condition throughout foraging trips ref [3]. Similarly, the duration and depth of dives are constrained by aerobic and anaerobic metabolic capacities, with the optimal allocation of time between travel, foraging, and surface intervals depending on the balance between these two pathways ref [5]. Digestive and thermal constraints also shape foraging behaviour, as the time required to process prey and maintain core temperature can limit the frequency and duration of foraging bouts ref [8]. These physiological limits are reflected in temporal patterns of foraging success: for example, stomach temperature telemetry in grey seals reveals that feeding events are distributed unevenly across the day, with individuals often consuming single large meals separated by long intervals, consistent with a batch-reactor digestive system ref [4]. Moreover, prolonged surfacing periods and drift dives observed in Baikal seals suggest that rest and food processing may occur simultaneously at sea, indicating that surface intervals are not merely recovery periods but may be integral to foraging success ref [2].

subsections.section_title: Inferring Foraging Behaviour from Single Data Types
subsections.subsection_title: Spatial and Temporal Scales of Foraging Inference from Movement Data
subsections.content:
Recently, Russell et al. ref [121] used an SSM to investigate the possible drivers of contrasting population trajectories for sympatric grey (Halichoerus grypus) and harbour seals in the North Sea. They combined location data with simultaneously-collected dive data. Using consistency in travel direction and displacement distance between temporally-regularised location fixes, the model identified between high transit rate with small changes in direction, and slower, more sinuous movement ref [121]. However, incorporating presence/absence of diving in the model allowed the authors to infer two behavioural states from slow movements; 'foraging', and 'resting at surface' ref [121].

Such state-space approaches have been widely adopted to disentangle complex movement patterns in marine predators, particularly when combined with environmental or physiological context ref [11]. The identification of area-restricted search (ARS) through first-passage time (FPT) analysis has proven effective in detecting foraging behaviour at multiple spatial scales, even in the presence of tracking error ref [2]. FPT has been shown to reveal the scale at which animals concentrate their search effort, with variance plots indicating optimal scales for foraging inference ref [1]. Moreover, the temporal structure of foraging bouts—such as the duration between patch encounters—can reflect prey patch distribution at fine and mesoscales, as demonstrated in Antarctic fur seals ref [9]. In marine predators, horizontal movement patterns derived from satellite tracking have been successfully linked to vertical foraging activity and foraging success, validating the use of surface movement as a proxy for diving behaviour ref [5]. However, the accuracy of inferring foraging from movement data is sensitive to sampling frequency and location error, with velocity filtering shown to mitigate these effects ref [2]. The robustness of state-space models in handling irregular sampling and non-Gaussian error structures further enhances their utility in extracting behavioural states from noisy tracking data ref [11]. Together, these methods underscore the importance of integrating spatial and temporal scales when interpreting foraging behaviour from movement data alone ref [1, 2, 5, 9, 11].

subsections.section_title: Inferring Foraging Behaviour from Single Data Types
subsections.subsection_title: Integrating Multi-Dimensional Data to Overcome Single-Data-Type Limitations
subsections.content:
Methods of inferring foraging from the data described above generally fall into three categories: (i) use of dive data, (ii) use of location data, and (iii) consideration of movements in three dimensions.

Methods of inferring foraging from the data described above generally fall into three categories: (i) use of dive data, (ii) use of location data, and (iii) consideration of movements in three dimensions.

In VHF studies during the early 1990s, the presence of diving was used to infer foraging activity in pinnipeds ref [32]. However, seals may dive for reasons other than searching for prey. For example, individuals may dive for efficient travel ref [31], and some species also perform resting or digestion dives ref [31, 35, 65, 66]. Diving datasets collected using pressure sensors can be applied in various ways to infer foraging. From each dive, a number of empirical and geometric measurements can be calculated, including the duration of the dive; duration of bottom time; maximum depth; duration of surface interval; ascent and descent rates; distribution of time allocation across depths (Time Allocation at Depth (TAD) index; see Glossary (Additional file 1)); and 2D dive profile shapes (Fig. 3). The application of each of these metrics depends on the resolution of the data, the temporal scale of analysis, and the specific research question (i.e. whether the study aims to quantify search activity, successful foraging or other aspects of behaviour and physiology).

To quantify foraging in terms of search behaviour at the scale of individual dives, ecologists have proposed that specific 2D dive profile shapes (representing depth over time) can be attributed to different behaviours (i.e. foraging, travelling and resting; Fig. 3b; [35,ref [67]ref [68]ref [69]). However, ground-truthing with direct metrics has revealed that the assumed link between dive shape and behaviour may not be consistent between species, age classes or lifehistory stages ref [15, 65]. The approach was first applied with northern elephant seals ref [35], and has subsequently been used for other species ref [31, 65, 70]. Benthic U-shaped dive profiles are thought to represent either stationary behaviour on, or movement along, the seabed, which have been interpreted as searching for or pursuing prey in benthicfeeding species ref [15], or resting at depth ref [31]. The presence of vertical 'wiggles' (sinuosity) during the bottom phase of U-shaped dives could also indicate active search behaviour, or pursuit of pelagic prey depending on the proximity to the seabed, and can be used to identify prey capture attempts within dives ref [28, 71]. However, the ability to detect these movements may be restricted to high-resolution datasets, and determining the proximity of an individual Fig. 3 Dive data. a Diagram of depth data collected at regular intervals throughout a dive (grey dashed line) and abstracted to inflection points for low resolution (blue dots) and high resolution (green dots) data. This abstraction may be performed using an algorithm on-board the device to reduce the amount of data stored and transmitted. b Different 2D dive profiles abstracted from dive data are often used to infer behaviour in seals. c Hypothetical example of how stomach temperature telemetry (STT) (top trace) can be used to validate assumptions of foraging inferred from dive profiles (bottom trace). Based on ref [15], Fig. 1. Arrow denotes feeding event, identified by sharp drop in stomach temperature to the seabed is often not possible with Argos-derived location data; accurately matching dive depth to the bathymetric depth of the location where that dive occurred requires a high frequency of accurate location estimates and high-resolution bathymetric data. Skewed shapes may represent drift-dives related to food processing, in which the seal is passively drifting through the water column ref [35, 72, 73]. V-shaped dives with no bottom time are often taken to represent travelling, or sampling the underwater environment ref [31, 65]. However, the geometry of a dive is affected by maximum dive depth; dives of similar bottom time may appear as either U or V-shaped depending on the depth. For example, elephant seals forage benthically on deep seamounts ref [74], and deep foraging dives may appear as V-shaped dives due to the extended time spent in descent and ascent relative to the bottom phase. A dive of similar bottom time at shallower depth with shorter ascent and descent phases would appear as a U-shaped dive.

Direct metrics of feeding have been used to evaluate the accuracy of dive profile shape analysis for identification of foraging. Kuhn et al. ref [15] used STT loggers to validate assumptions of behaviour from dive profiles for northern elephant seals (Fig. 3c) and found that, although most common on U-shaped wiggle dives (74.2 % of feeding events), feeding occurred on dives of all shapes. Baechler et al. ref [65] used animal-borne cameras coupled with TDRs, to observe search behaviour in both male and female harbour seals of varying age class. They found that U-shaped dives were a reasonable predictor of search activity for most individuals. However, the accuracy of predicting search behaviour from dive shapes varied for males during the breeding season. Matching video footage with TDR data revealed adult males producing U-shaped dive profiles whilst searching for prey, travelling and roaring underwater (a vocalisation behaviour associated with reproduction) ref [65]. 2D profiles do not account for lateral displacement underwater; i.e. if an individual remains at constant depth, from a 2D shape we cannot deduce whether they are actively searching or remaining stationary (due to resting, vocalisation, or waiting to ambush prey for example). 3D reconstruction of dives using acoustic positioning arrays, video recorders and accelerometers has revealed that pinniped foraging behaviour during a dive can be remarkably varied and complex ref [18, 75, 76]. Reconstruction suggests that, if used as the sole analytical technique, 2D profiles may be overly simplistic, introducing a degree of subjectivity to classification of behaviours. Triaxial accelerometers can be particularly helpful to improve our understanding of 3D movement underwater. Head-mounted accelerometers have been used to identify prey-capture attempts in multiple species ref [12, 71, 77]. However, they can also be used to determine body position and horizontal displacement, and potentially elucidate the particular behaviours associated with individual dives ref [78]. For example, Sala et. al. ref [78] deployed TDRs with integrated accelerometers on elephant seals to assess the accuracy of behavioural assumptions from 2D dive shapes. By including data on pitch and roll, the authors were able to visualise the body position of individuals at all phases of dives, and differentiate more effectively between passive drift dives, and active search dives ref [78]. Moving forwards, combining accelerometer data with dive and location data will increase our ability to infer search behaviour and feeding attempts in 3D. However, accelerometers generate large volumes of data, and the successful transmission of such a quantity of data is currently challenging. Therefore, the deployment of accelerometers is largely restricted to scenarios where they can be recovered. For studies in developed areas, integration of accelerometers into GPS-GSM tags may provide a future solution to this problem.

Whilst U-shaped dives have been used to infer search behaviour at the scale of individual dives, resting dives (with a right or left-skewed shape) may be useful for identifying successful foraging over a broader temporal scale. Drift-rate during rest dives is correlated with an individual's buoyancy in elephant seals, allowing the inference of body mass gain due to successful foraging ref [79]. In this way, areas of successful foraging can be mapped ref [80, 81] and other methods of inferring foraging success from location and dive data can be evaluated ref [82, 83]. Although similar right and left-skewed dive profiles have been reported in other species ref [65, 66], comparable relationships between drift-rate and mass gain are yet to be described. This discovery has yielded a relatively simple method of assessing foraging success for long-ranging animals without the need for identifying foraging behaviour. However, phocid seals experience dramatic changes in body mass and composition in response to life-history events, such as fasting (i.e. the post-weaning fast in pups, or due to being hauled out for moulting or reproduction in adults), pupping, and season ref [84]. Following a period of mass loss, an individual may gain lean mass rather than blubber ref [85, 86]. Changes in pinniped body composition may also be affected by the lipid content of their prey-type ref [87, 88], or by seasonal changes in the amount of blubber needed for thermoregulation ref [89]. In this case, although the individual may be foraging successfully, it is unlikely to experience a positive buoyancy change because lean mass is denser than water ref [84, 86]. Using drift dives to infer foraging success thus has the potential to overlook successful foraging in some circumstances.

In addition to using dive profiles, ecologists have built theoretical foraging models using dive metrics such as dive frequency, depth, bottom duration, ascent and descent rates, as well as duration of post-dive intervals. Using these models, foraging success is inferred based on assumptions drawn from OFT. Pinnipeds must dive in order to search for food, and the descent and ascent phases of a dive represent the transit to and from a prey patch ref [90]. OFT dictates that individuals will concentrate their time in areas of successful feeding ref [1]. Following this, and based on the assumption that foraging occurs during the bottom phase of dives ref [15, 91, 92], optimal diving theory (ODT) suggests that divers will maximise their time at the bottom phase of a foraging dive ref [93]. By maximising time spent at foraging depth, and minimising the time spent in transit (descent and ascent) and recovery (post-dive surface interval), individuals increase their chances of prey capture, offsetting the energetic costs of transit between the surface and the prey patch ref [93]. Importantly, from this perspective, time underwater is maximised over bouts (a succession of foraging dives with minimal surface interval) rather than individual dives ref [93]. Exceeding the aerobic dive limit (ADL; the point at which lactate begins to build up in the blood ref [94]) on a single dive, or successive short aerobic dives, will result in anaerobic metabolism, increasing recovery time at the surface and potentially decreasing net energetic gain ref [2, 95, 96]. Theoretical foraging models based on ODT predict that oxygen will be the limiting factor in dive behaviour ref [96], and that individuals will consistently dive up to their calculated ADL during foraging dives in order to maximise prey-capture opportunities. Such models therefore predict that foraging success increases with dive duration, bottom time and dive frequency ref [83].

However, such theoretical foraging models do not account for many of the ecological and physiological complexities that may regulate predator diving. For example, an individual's physiological capacity to dive to, and remain at depth may vary on a seasonal and diurnal scale ref [97]. Therefore, predators may adapt their foraging strategies to account for this physiological plasticity. Furthermore, ODT models assume that prey patches are of a uniform density and quality. In reality this is not the case, and depending on the quality and depth of a prey patch, and the level of competition from other predators, maximising time at foraging depth may not always be the most energy-efficient foraging strategy ref [91, 98]. For example, in an area with a high density of good quality prey patches where prey capture rates are high, the need to stay at depth is less acute; individuals may surface and move on to a new prey patch with lower energetic consequences. The decision to move on may be driven by localised depletion of the food resource, competition, or the need to rest and digest ref [99]. Likewise, Sparling et. al. ref [98] have shown that individuals that abandon search and move on early in areas of low prey density maximise net energetic gain. Therefore, in these scenarios, increased bottom time is not correlated with foraging success. Direct observations of feeding attempts have been used to test the performance of ODT models as predictors of foraging success. Such studies have shown that the accuracy of different predictor variables may vary between species, habitats and temporal scale of analysis ref [21]ref [22]ref [23]ref [24, 100]. Viviant et al. ref [23] deployed accelerometers (measuring jaw-openings as a proxy for prey capture attempts) in conjunction with TDRs on Antarctic fur seals (Arctocephalus gazella). They tested a combination of metrics including bottom duration, ascent and descent rates and maximum dive depth as predictors of foraging success. Ground-truthing with accelerometer data revealed that the best predictors varied depending on the temporal scale of analysis, ranging from individual dives to several hours ref [23]. This suggests that data resolution is likely to be a key factor in the accuracy of different methods of identifying foraging success from dive metrics; the best predictor of foraging success for a particular dive bout may not perform as well when applied across an entire foraging trip. With this in mind, current theoretical foraging models using dive metrics may be too simplistic to accurately describe the dynamics of decision-making in foraging behaviour.

Overall, dive data are a powerful resource when attempting to quantify foraging effort in pinnipeds, in which direct observations of search behaviour or feeding attempts are not available, but should be used with a clear understanding of their limitations. Recent studies suggest that highresolution dive datasets can be used to inform the best analytical approach for low-resolution data ref [30, 101]. Moving forwards, tagging a sub-sample of animals with high-resolution devices, cameras or accelerometers where possible may be a good option for future studies in order to identify appropriate analytical techniques.

Animal location data can be used to identify and quantify foraging. For central place foragers that make discrete foraging trips to sea, returning to land to rest and digest, or provision young, the duration and extent of these trips are used to make broad observations of foraging effort ref [102]ref [103]ref [104]. However, in isolation, trip duration and extent give no information about where individuals are searching for prey, how they are exploiting their environment in order to find it, what proportion of the time at sea is spent foraging in relation to other behaviours such as resting and travelling, and if they are foraging successfully. Within the trip itself, the distribution of time along the track can be analysed, and movement patterns that may relate to specific behaviours can be identified ref [105]. The simplest way to deconstruct a horizontal track and identify movement patterns is to divide it into segments of straight lines interrupted by turns. In order to quantify the distribution of time along a track, it is often necessary to regularise 'fixes' (locations) to a constant time step (Fig. 4a). By interpolating between temporally-regularised locations, the displacement distance and change in bearing between fixes can then be extracted (Fig. 4b). Displacement gives a measure of ground speed, whilst change in bearing (turning angle) can show track sinuosity. Predator movements are often classified into two broad strategies; ref [1] 'directed' travel with little or no meandering, and ref [2] 'resident' behaviour with slower, meandering movement (Fig. 5a) ref [105, 106]. In the context of OFT, these slower movements are commonly attributed to area-restricted search (ARS) behaviour, indicative of foraging effort within a prey patch ref [105, 107, 108]. Studies commonly use track metrics to distinguish between directed and resident movement patterns. For example, travel to and from, or between, foraging patches is associated with high displacement between fixes, and small changes in bearing. In contrast, ARS behaviour is characterised by a more sinuous track section with lower displacement ref [105]. Although opportunistic foraging may occur during directed travel ref [15, 31, 109], and individuals may search for prey on multiple spatial scales ref [108, 110], ARS behaviour is often used to quantify when and where predators concentrate foraging effort. Methods of quantifying ARS from track metrics range from simple descriptive approaches (e.g. plotting variable distributions through time and defining a threshold ref [106]) to sophisticated mechanistic models that can incorporate multiple movement metrics at different data resolutions and account for spatial uncertainty of location estimates ref [111].

As an alternative to the use of displacement and turning angle, first-passage time (FPT) can be used to distinguish between ARS and directed movement ref [107]. The FPT is defined as the time taken for an individual to cross a virtual circle of given radius ref [107]. The circle is centred on the location fix, and the FPT is calculated by summing the number of temporally-regularised time steps taken to leave the circle boundary in both forward and backward directions (Fig. 5b). The areas in which individuals concentrate their time can be identified by sliding this circle along the track (Fig. 5c). FPT analysis is conceptually simple and relatively straightforward to implement. Nevertheless, certain limitations restrict its accuracy for pinnipeds. For example, Fauchald and Tveraa ref [107] proposed that the chosen radius of the circle should be equal to the diameter of a typical prey patch. This, however, assumes that all prey patches will be circular, and of equal density, and that predators are repelled by patch boundaries. In reality, the density and distribution of pinniped prey resources is rarely known, and may vary along a single track. Seals may access multiple habitats, and target different prey types during a foraging trip, with subsequent effects on foraging behaviour and the scale of search ref [108, 112]. The circle radius chosen for FPT analysis will therefore be somewhat arbitrary, and defining one scale for the entire track may be inappropriate ref [108].

'Residence time' (RT) analysis was developed as an adaptation of the FPT concept to attempt to overcome the aforementioned limitation. It can take account of previous time spent in the same circle (Fig. 5b) ref [108]. This means that the analysis is more effective at identifying foraging areas in heterogeneous environments, as it gives a cumulative measure of habitat use ref [108]. Furthermore, RT analysis uses a statistical approach (penalised contrast algorithm; ref [113]) to identify ARS, rather than relying on visual inspection of model output ref [108]. Barraquand and Benhamou ref [108] show that the RT approach is also less influenced by data resolution than FPT analysis. Whilst this method represents a step forward from FPT analysis, it still relies on the user to define certain parameters (i.e. the amount of time an animal is out of the circle before that path segment is discounted; Fig. 5b). Furthermore, as with FPT, RT analysis cannot account for the uncertainty related to location estimates, or give a measure of uncertainty related to assumptions of foraging behaviour. In recent years, sophisticated modelling techniques have been developed that can perform these functions in a more objective manner ref [111]. a In order to calculate changes in track metrics through time, it is often necessary to regularise recorded 'fixes' (locations) to a constant time step. The resulting regularised fixes are normally connected in space with linear interpolation. b Diagram shows two metrics commonly used in movement analyses. Change in bearing (turning angle) is a measure of path sinuosity, whilst the displacement distance between temporally-regularised location fixes can give an estimate of ground speed. By examining changes to these metrics over time different movement patterns can be identified State-space models (SSMs) have multiple applications for animal movement studies ref [111, 114]. SSMs can be used to improve the spatial accuracy of location estimates, and/or estimate movement modes ref [115]. Location estimates can be processed with an SSM (e.g. Kalman filter; KF) to reduce spatial errors ref [116]. The SSM predicts the current state (location) together with its associated spatial error. For data collected since 2008, Argos have offered the option to receive location estimates derived by a KF, rather than the original least squares (LS) algorithm ref [46]. Once a prediction for a location is made, the algorithm updates all predictions of previous locations using a weighted average, giving more weight to estimates with higher certainty. Recent studies have tested the accuracy of both KF-derived and LS-derived Argos locations for phocids using simultaneously collected high-resolution Fastloc® GPS data as a measure of 'true' location ref [50, 51]. Silva et al. ref [51] found that 82 % of KFderived harbour seal locations were within 5 km of the 'true' GPS positions, compared with 73 % of LS-derived locations. By improving location accuracy, SSMs can increase the potential of low resolution telemetry datasets for investigation of behaviours ref [50, 51].

SSMs have been developed that can estimate movement modes from location data. The cleaning of the location data, to improve accuracy, can be combined with state estimation ref [115, 117]. Alternatively, data are used directly for state estimation within a hidden Markov model (HMM); such data must be spatially accurate (GPS-derived), or already cleaned using an SSM to improve accuracy ref [111]. HMMs are SSMs in which a finite number of discrete states are defined. States are estimated based on the distribution of movement metrics through time ref [118]. HMMs take input movement metrics, such as displacement and consistency in travel direction, and generate unique posterior distributions for each, based on a specified or estimated number of behavioural states (Fig. 5d). A recently-developed R package "moveHMM" makes building ML HMMs accessible for researchers outside the field of statistics ref [119].

SSMs represent a powerful tool for foraging analysis in that they can combine multiple movement metrics from tracking data and estimate movement states with a higher degree of statistical robustness than other commonly-used methods ref [111, 117, 120]. For example, unlike FPT and RT approaches, SSMs can distinguish between multiple movement patterns without needing to apply thresholds to movement metrics or analytical scale ref [117]. Using biological rationale, ecologists infer behaviours from the discrete movement states identified by the SSM. SSMs enable us to quantify foraging behaviour in relation to other behaviours such as resting and travelling, and thus tackle a Two patterns of movement can typically be detected in predator tracks; extensive movements with high displacement and low turning angle (grey lines) and intensive movements with low displacement and high turning angles (blue lines). Intensive movements are commonly taken to represent area-restricted search (ARS) behaviour. b Fist-passage time (FPT) is the sum of temporally-regularised location fixes required to leave a circle of given radius in both forward and backward directions from time point t i (yellow dots). Residence time (RT) includes total time spent in the circle from present (iii-iv), previous (i-ii) and future (v-vi) time steps (green lines), provided that time outside the circle (gap between intersection points ii-iii or between iv-v) is not above a user-defined threshold. c Areas of high FPT / RT can be identified by sliding the circle along the track at each time step. Red dashes denote the areas in space (left) and time (right) taken to represent ARS. d Demonstration of a three-state HMM output. Right-hand plot shows posterior Weibull distributions of displacement for three discrete states. Using biological rationale, movement states can be used to infer behaviours (e.g. state 3 with high displacement may be travelling, states 1 and 2 may be either foraging or resting). Presence/absence of diving can be included in the model to distinguish between foraging and resting at the surface ref [121] more complex questions of how these activities interact through time and space [117,ref [121]ref [122]ref [123]. Importantly, models can test the influence of explanatory covariates on the probability of switching into a certain movement state. For example, Morales et al. ref [124] demonstrated how SSMs can be used to investigate the influence of environmental factors on foraging decisions. Furthermore, models can be applied in either a frequentist Maximum Likelihood (ML) or Bayesian framework. Although ML models are more tractable and computationally less costly, they typically require data to be in uniform time steps with little associated error in order to make the calculation ref [118]. Bayesian models do not have such constraints, and therefore can account for spatial uncertainty and irregular time series arising from coarse tracking data ref [114]. This makes them a good option for data collected via the Argos system. However, processing time for Bayesian models is greatly increased due to the associated computational demand.

Pinniped location data has been an important resource for developing and testing the utility of SSMs for animal movement studies ref [117]. SSMs have now been applied to large datasets to investigate diverse questions including intrinsic and extrinsic drivers of variation in foraging behaviour ref [121, 122]. However, despite the relative advantages of SSM approaches over other commonly-used analytical methods, they share a common limitation if only applied to location data. Using only horizontal movements, these techniques assume that individuals make discrete journeys in order to forage, but return to the central place to rest. This paradigm therefore assumes only two behavioural modes at sea; travelling and foraging, and attributes all slow, sinuous movements to ARS behaviour ref [117, 122]. Given that many pinniped species rest at sea during foraging trips either at the surface ref [31, 105, 121, 125], or beneath it ref [66, 72], producing similar movement patterns to ARS, using location data in this way may over-estimate foraging behaviour. In order to overcome these limitations it is necessary to consider movement in three dimensions.

Recently, Russell et al. ref [121] used an SSM to investigate the possible drivers of contrasting population trajectories for sympatric grey (Halichoerus grypus) and harbour seals in the North Sea. They combined location data with simultaneously-collected dive data. Using consistency in travel direction and displacement distance between temporally-regularised location fixes, the model identified between high transit rate with small changes in direction, and slower, more sinuous movement ref [121]. However, incorporating presence/absence of diving in the model allowed the authors to infer two behavioural states from slow movements; 'foraging', and 'resting at surface' ref [121].

Moreover, where previous studies had excluded data within proximity of the coast to avoid classifying time spent hauled out on land as foraging, using the dive data, they were able to include resting on land as a further behaviour in their analysis of activity budgets ref [121]. In this way, the analysis was able to capture coastal foraging that may have been excluded by applying a coastal buffer ref [121]. Importantly, the study found that >10 % of the seals' activity was attributed to resting at the surface whilst at sea, highlighting the importance of combining track metrics with dive data to ensure that resting behaviour is not mistakenly classified as foraging ref [121]. For species that commonly rest underwater, however, such as elephant seals, incorporation of presence/absence of diving would not be a satisfactory method of distinguishing between resting and foraging. In this case, models could attempt to distinguish resting dives by their shape, duration or vertical displacement rate compared to foraging or travelling dives, and thus inform behavioural states in the same way.

Although either dive or location data may be used in isolation to identify foraging with traditional methods or SSMs, the accuracy of analysis is often scale-dependent and highly influenced by data resolution. Furthermore, using one of these data types alone may over-simplify atsea behaviours, leading to over or under-estimation of foraging activity. Including both dive and location metrics in analytical models lends more information, and therefore more power to foraging analysis ref [126]. Bestley et al. ref [120] incorporated dive depth and duration, as well as post-dive surface interval into an SSM with horizontal track metrics to describe foraging for multiple Antarctic pinniped species. The use of vertical data improved the capacity of the model to identify where foraging bouts occurred ref [120]. Increasing the accuracy of foraging models in this way will allow ecologists to identify important foraging habitat with greater certainty, and improve the effectiveness of conservation management. Moving forwards, SSMs represent a powerful tool for tackling complex questions of both the spatial and energetic dynamics of foraging. Furthermore, the ability to incorporate environmental covariates in SSMs may prove vital in unravelling how oceanographic processes drive spatial and temporal patterns of foraging behaviour ref [114, 127, 128]. SSMs have great potential for maximising the utility of tracking datasets, and the combined advantages they offer cannot currently be equalled by any other approach that we know of. SSM techniques not only allow us to identify foraging behaviour in a more statistically robust manner than traditional methods, but they allow us to do so by combining multiple data types (e.g. dive and location data) and qualities (e.g. Argos and GPS data) in the same analysis, thus maximising the application of available data resources ref [61, 121]. However, a trade-off exists between the computational tractability and simplicity of models, and biological realism. For example, combining multiple data types will improve the biological realism of inferred behavioural states, but will increase computational demand and technical complexity. Nevertheless, SSMs for animal tracking data continue to be refined and developed, and these models represent our best option for improving our understanding of pinniped foraging dynamics as multi-year tracking datasets grow in abundance. This progress will depend, however, on ecologists collaborating closely with statisticians, sharing their code openly alongside published studies.

Environmental variability, including climatic anomalies, can profoundly influence the foraging ecology and provisioning strategies of pinnipeds, with consequences for reproductive success and population dynamics ref [48]. For instance, interannual shifts in sea-surface temperature and prey availability linked to large-scale climate events such as the El Niño Southern Oscillation have been shown to alter diving depth, foraging zone location, and efficiency in Antarctic fur seals ref [48]. These oceanographic fluctuations can disrupt the temporal match between lactation periods and peak marine productivity, thereby constraining energy acquisition for pups ref [48]. Beyond direct physiological impacts, climate-driven changes in habitat structure and prey distribution may also force individuals to adjust their spatial range and movement patterns, as observed across multiple pinniped species ref [16]. Long-term demographic studies further reveal that survival trends in southern elephant seals are influenced by the interplay between environmental conditions, such as the Southern Oscillation Index, and population density, highlighting the cascading effects of climate variability on life-history outcomes ref [50]. Similarly, temporal and spatial variation in survival rates of Hawaiian monk seals across their archipelagic range underscores how regional climate and oceanographic conditions can differentially affect age-specific viability, even within a single species ref [15]. The integration of animal-borne sensors, such as CTD-Satellite Relay Data Loggers, has enabled real-time monitoring of oceanographic conditions experienced by foraging pinnipeds, providing critical context for interpreting behavioral responses to environmental change ref [10]. Moreover, large-scale satellite tagging programs have demonstrated that foraging behavior in species like the harbor seal is strongly structured by local habitat conditions and proximity to productive foraging grounds, rather than intrinsic factors alone, suggesting that climate-induced shifts in ocean productivity may directly reshape spatial use patterns ref [11].

subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Integration: Linking Behavior to Environment
subsections.content: (age / sex classes, sample size, population, representativeness, accessibility) ref [54], ref [5], ref [53]

The vast majority of marine predator studies that recreate animal movements from tracking data do so in geographical space; i.e. they assume that the individual is moving through a still medium with no physical forces acting upon them. The reality is that ocean tides and currents can have a strong and dynamic influence on movement and therefore how we infer behaviour [ref [57]]. Gaspar et al. [ref [57]] reconstructed the movements of a migrating leatherback turtle (Dermochelys coriacea) in both geographical and hydrographical space (accounting for ocean currents). They showed that currents can have a large influence on how we interpret track tortuosity, and therefore identify ARS. The study demonstrated how overlooking ocean currents can compromise our ability to successfully identify foraging activity, particularly in areas of high turbulence which are normally associated with high prey density and productivity [ref [57]].

Empirical studies on pinnipeds confirm that tidal dynamics directly structure foraging behavior: harbour seals (Phoca vitulina) aggregate near channel constrictions during flood tides, with peak foraging activity coinciding with slower flooding currents and higher capture rates of salmon and forage fish [ref [56]]. This pattern is further supported by telemetry data showing intensive, non-random use of narrow coastal channels modulated by tidal phase, with seals maximizing time in areas of enhanced prey encounter probability during flood tides [ref [57]]. Such tidal modulation of habitat use is not limited to adults; juvenile Australian sea lions (Neophoca cinerea) exhibit restricted spatial foraging ranges in shallow coastal waters, where tidal currents and bathymetry interact to constrain access to prey, potentially increasing vulnerability to environmental change [ref [5]].

Although we are drawing an increasingly detailed picture of marine predator foraging behaviour, research has tended to be heavily focussed on a handful of species and demographic classes ref [26, 152]. In pinniped tracking studies, there is a general bias towards reproductive females ref [152], as many species are tied to land throughout the pupping and provisioning phase of the breeding cycle, and are thus easier to catch for tag application and retrieval. This is most notable in the otariid literature. Nevertheless, foraging strategies are known to vary seasonally, between the sexes ref [104, 122, 153, 154, 155], age classes ref [123, 156, 157, 158], and indeed between individuals in general ref [92, 112, 159]. Due to cost and logistics, tagging studies are often constrained by relatively small sample sizes. However, in order to answer research questions that will have some benefit to the conservation management of species, it is often necessary to make population-level inferences about foraging and habitat use ref [160]. Fully understanding population dynamics and potential threats may therefore depend on examining the behaviour of individuals from across their range, sexes and age classes ref [160]. A further consideration is that the individuals selected for a tagging study may not always be representative of the wider population. Logistical constraints mean that tagged animals are rarely selected at random. For example, it may be necessary to select individuals from the periphery of a colony in order to minimise disturbance, or known animals may be preferentially selected based on their contribution to long-term datasets, or robustness to handling. However, it is not known how the capture or selection method may introduce bias to population-level inferences of behaviour; i.e. animals taken from the periphery of a colony may be in poorer condition, which may be reflected in their behaviour at sea. Moving forwards, when investigating population-level foraging, researchers should consider the number of tags that need to be deployed, and whether they can logistically obtain a balanced and representative sample (Fig. 6). For a more detailed discussion on representativeness of study sample in population-level tracking studies, see ref [160].

Oceanographic drivers such as fronts, temperature gradients, and current systems have been shown to structure prey distributions and thereby shape foraging behaviour across marine predators. For instance, basking sharks in the north-east Atlantic exhibit strong associations with thermal and chlorophyll-a fronts, where zooplankton aggregations enhance foraging opportunities ref [4]. Similarly, mesoscale fronts have been identified as critical foraging habitats for pelagic seabirds, with composite front mapping revealing consistent habitat use patterns linked to oceanographic interfaces ref [5]. In bottlenose dolphins, fine-scale foraging movements are concentrated near small-scale hydrographic fronts and areas of steep seabed topography, suggesting that predator-prey interactions are mediated by local hydrodynamics ref [3]. Southern elephant seals from the Kerguelen Islands target specific oceanographic zones—particularly near the Polar Front and Antarctic continental shelf—where increased foraging activity and improved body condition correlate with distinct temperature signatures and dive patterns ref [7]. These findings are reinforced by studies showing that neglecting ocean currents in tracking data analysis can distort the identification of foraging areas and misrepresent energy expenditure, underscoring the necessity of integrating in situ oceanographic conditions into behavioural interpretations ref [2]. Furthermore, variations in the behaviour and condition of Southern Ocean top predators are directly linked to in situ oceanographic features, highlighting the role of environmental heterogeneity in driving foraging success ref [1].

subsections.subsection_title: Intrinsic Factors: Sex, Age, and Body Condition
subsections.content:
As we continue to impact marine ecosystems with overfishing; increased vessel traffic; habitat modification; pollution, and anthropogenic climate change, rates of biodiversity loss may pass a critical threshold of extinction ref [173]. In addition to these pressures, the ramifications for marine fauna of policy changes such as fisheries discard reforms, and the switch from hydrocarbon extraction to marine renewable energy installations, remain unknown. Assessing the significance of these changes for marine ecosystems will be of chief importance for conservation management ref [173, 174]. Among the species likely to be most immediately and obviously affected are marine predators ref [19, 130, 175]. Accurately reconstructing predator foraging movements will be crucial to identifying critical habitat for marine species and designing effective Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) that will benefit entire ecosystems ref [176]ref [177]ref [178]ref [179]. Moreover, marine mammals represent a valuable resource as sentinels of ecosystem health, and expanding our knowledge of their foraging behaviour will allow us to assess how marine systems may respond under global environmental change ref [180]ref [181]ref [182]ref [183]. Biologging data will no doubt play a leading role in this process, and further refining analytical techniques of these data should be given high priority ref [144]. There remain inherent limitations in inferring animal behaviour from location and dive data. No one analytical approach can capture foraging from these data with complete accuracy. However, ecologists can select the best analytical method based upon several key considerations; the research question, the study species, the number and class of individuals required, the device type, and device programming (Fig. 6). Depending on the range of movement of the individual, the resolution of the data and the complexity of the analysis, some techniques may over or under-estimate foraging. Nevertheless, SSMs represent a rapidly-developing holistic statistical method that has the capacity to incorporate multiple data types and allows more robust behavioural inferences to be made ref [111]. SSMs will allow ecologists to create a more complete picture of activity budgets and population dynamics ref [121, 122], with the potential to draw links between predator behaviours and environmental phenomena ref [128]. The priority for future work is to focus on incorporating oceanographic information into analyses to better understand patterns of habitat use, to determine the physical and behavioural consequences of specific tags to the study animal, and to develop an understanding of the ontogeny of foraging strategies in naïve pups. This will lead to more accurate population-level assessment of habitat use and will therefore benefit our ability to mitigate the effects of anthropogenic activity on the marine environment.

Intrinsic factors such as sex, age, and body condition profoundly shape foraging behaviour in pinnipeds. Studies on grey and harbour seals have demonstrated that sex and body size significantly influence foraging-trip duration, range, and time spent at sea, with females exhibiting shorter trips and smaller foraging ranges compared to males, likely due to reproductive constraints and energy allocation strategies ref [1, 2]. These patterns are further corroborated in grey seals, where sex-specific foraging tactics, revealed through state-space analysis, align with sexual size dimorphism and dietary differences, indicating that males and females respond differently to seasonal prey availability and reproductive costs ref [3]. Such sex-based divergence is also reflected in diet composition, with adult males consuming a more diverse but less energy-dense diet than females, particularly during the post-breeding period when females prioritize energy storage for pregnancy and lactation ref [5]. Dive behaviour further reflects these intrinsic differences: female grey seals exhibit higher dive effort, longer dives, and greater time spent at depth during critical reproductive windows, while males show more consistent, less diurnally constrained diving patterns, suggesting divergent strategies in energy accumulation ref [6]. The development of foraging strategies with age is equally critical; juvenile grey seals, despite navigating as effectively as adults, undertake longer foraging trips with greater transit times to reach foraging areas, indicating higher foraging effort and a learning curve in spatial efficiency ref [4]. Similar ontogenetic patterns are observed in Galapagos sea lions, where juveniles exhibit distinct diving strategies and delayed independence in foraging, particularly under adverse environmental conditions such as El Niño events, highlighting the interaction between age, experience, and environmental variability ref [8]. In gray seal pups, the development of diving capabilities during the postweaning fast is strongly influenced by age at departure and body mass, with heavier pups achieving higher peak dive performance and longer survival, while smaller pups face trade-offs between early performance and long-term resilience ref [9]. Collectively, these findings underscore that sex, age, and body condition are not merely covariates but central determinants of foraging ecology, necessitating their explicit integration into models of habitat use and population dynamics.
